contentHtml:
Proposes GST neutrality, a preventive screening tax deduction and a ₹1,00,000 crore financing window to make quality care more affordable and available beyond the metros

NATHEALTH–Healthcare Federation of India, has submitted its pre-budget recommendations for the Union Budget 2027–28 to the Government of India. The 12-point agenda is led by a proposed Rs 1,00,000 crore Healthcare Infrastructure and Resilience Window to ease high capital costs and limited long-tenor finance. It rests on a simple belief: as India moves from Swasth Bharat to Viksit Bharat, healthcare has to be built as an enabler of growth and not just a service that follows it.

Over the years, India’s healthcare sector has expanded its capacity, adopted new technology and widened its reach. The next phase calls for more. Quality care must be available beyond the metros, and it must be affordable. Health systems must be digitally connected and supported by a skilled workforce. India must also be able to innovate and to serve patients and markets beyond its borders. Delivering this will need sustained collaboration between government and industry, and the recommendations are framed to make that partnership work.

NATHEALTH’s submission therefore proposes a patient-centred compact between government and the healthcare sector. Public finance would de-risk priority investments, strengthen the purchasing of healthcare services and draw private investment into areas of national importance. This approach is aimed at improving the affordability and availability of quality care for patients, while ensuring that public resources are deployed effectively and deliver measurable value. Government support would be linked to clearly defined commitments on service delivery in underserved regions, quality standards, patient safety, price transparency, financial accountability and health outcomes.

Dr Sangita Reddy, President, NATHEALTH and Joint Managing Director, Apollo Hospitals Group, said,“A nation’s growth story is only as strong as the health of its people. As India sets its sights on Viksit Bharat, healthcare can no longer be seen as something that follows growth. It has to be built as an enabler of it. The sector has the capability and the willingness to invest, and government has the vision and the reach. Our recommendations are an invitation to bring the two together, around a shared commitment to what patients experience at the end of it. This also means building on India’s potential as a global healthcare destination by operationalising the Medical Value Travel hubs announced in the previous Union Budget, and creating a more integrated, seamless experience for international patients.”

Himanshu Baid, Senior Vice President, NATHEALTH and Managing Director, Poly Medicure Ltd, said,” We sincerely appreciate the Govt.’s visionary initiative to strengthen the domestic medical devices industry through the launch of the PLI Scheme. This landmark intervention will accelerate indigenous manufacturing, drive innovation, attract investments and enhance India’s competitiveness as a global MedTech manufacturing hub. India has the talent, the manufacturing base and the clinical depth to be more than a large healthcare market. We can be a trusted source of healthcare solutions for the world. That ambition needs a policy environment in which investors, innovators and providers can plan for the long term with confidence. A healthcare system that is strong at home will also give India the credibility to compete abroad.”

Varun Khanna, Vice President, NATHEALTH and Managing Director & Group CEO, Aster DM Quality Care Ltd, added, “Strengthening India’s healthcare infrastructure requires a long-term approach that brings together adequate financing, quality-focused investments and a sustainable operating environment. Investments in hospital infrastructure, technology and clinical capability, particularly in underserved and emerging regions, are ultimately investments in outcomes for patients: faster recovery, fewer complications and quality care closer to home. When the high cost of capital eases, the benefit does not stay with providers alone. It translates into more affordable care and better value for every rupee a patient spends. NATHEALTH’s proposed Healthcare Infrastructure and Resilience Window is a step in this direction. Equally important is an enabling policy framework that recognises quality, patient safety, transparency and measurable health outcomes, so that better care and sustainable economics move together. A stronger healthcare delivery ecosystem will improve access, affordability and quality of care for patients, and advance India’s ambition of building a resilient healthcare system aligned with Viksit Bharat 2047.”

NATHEALTH’s key recommendations for Union Budget 2027–28

Priority

Recommendation

What NATHEALTH proposes

Building capacity and easing costs

1. Rs 1,00,000 crore Healthcare Infrastructure and Resilience Window

A dedicated financing window combining long-term debt, credit enhancement and selective viability-gap funding, with flexible conditions on quality, accreditation, transparency and access.

Connecting systems and preventing disease

2. Accelerate adoption of digital health

Time-bound incentives for smaller providers to adopt interoperable records, consent-based data exchange, cybersecurity and integrated workflows, along with an NHCX-based claims-discounting solution.

3. Prevention and NCD Outcomes Mission

Co-funded, outcome-linked NCD programmes, and an annual tax deduction of up to ₹10,000 for eligible preventive screenings. Screening would be judged by diagnosis, treatment and follow-up, not by tests conducted.

Quality and financial protection

4. Benchmark and report quality and clinical indicators

Quality cells in national and state health assurance trusts to drive empanelment of accredited providers and a movement on patient safety and outcomes.

5. Expand financial protection beyond hospitalisation

A standardised, actuarially priced base insurance product for the “missing middle”, and pilots for outpatient and chronic-care coverage.

Building the workforce

6. Use healthcare delivery networks for workforce training

Recognition of eligible hospitals, diagnostic centres and home-care providers as supervised training and assessment sites, with funding linked to training, competency, placement and retention outcomes.

7. Strengthen availability of professionals beyond major cities

Time-bound incentives for critical cadres in shortage districts, and expanded DNB training and specialist rotations through hospital networks.

Innovation and MedTech

8. Rs 5,000 crore HealthTech and MedTech Translational Platform

Competitive grants, challenge-based funding and co-investment for clinical validation, regulatory readiness, evidence generation and commercial scale-up.

Competing globally

9. “Heal in India” as a measurable services export mission

A performance-linked annual market-development fund of Rs 750 crore for international payer partnerships, visa facilitation and an integrated patient journey.

10. Accelerate healthcare and MedTech exports

Export credit support, certification assistance and facilitation of regulatory approvals in priority markets, especially for eligible MSMEs.
